source: Thorndike & Woodworth (1901) The influence of improvement in one mental function upon the efficiency of other functions
finding: Founding paper. Trained people to estimate areas of one shape set, then tested other shapes and other functions. Transfer appeared only where the two tasks shared parts.
numbers: About 125 paper pieces. Series 1: 13 rectangles 20-90 sq cm. Series 2: 27 triangles, circles, irregular figures. Training on rectangles 10-100 sq cm, 1000-2000 trials. Gain was larger for similar shapes than for different shapes in every subject but one (Be). Small N, per-subject reports.
quote: spread of practice occurs only where identical elements are concerned in the influencing and influenced function
limits: Tiny sample, no control group by modern standards. Result is graded: some transfer to other shapes still occurred. Table values were not readable in the text.
agent_relevance: Lesson reuse should be judged by shared parts (same sub-operation, same data form), not by topic label.

source: Thorndike & Woodworth (1901), mechanism of the transfer that did occur
finding: The authors explain the observed transfer by shared components: a better mental standard for one rectangle helped judge other shapes, and the habit of correcting a known bias was a shared element across functions.
numbers: Also cited: Wissler found little correlation among tested functions; Norsworthy found no correlation between misspelling detection and multiplication accuracy or speed.
quote: The mind is, on the contrary, on its dynamic side a machine for making particular reactions to particular situations.
limits: Elements were never formally defined, so the theory is hard to falsify: any transfer can be named an identical element after the fact.
agent_relevance: A lesson card should name the shared element it relies on (a bias to correct, a standard to compare against), so reuse can be checked.

source: Thorndike & Woodworth (1901), statistical treatment
finding: The authors used probable-error arguments to show training effects were not chance.
numbers: Areas 41 and 42 sq cm: mean-square errors 6.2 and 3.1; difference 2.6 times the probable difference. One series had 31 differences above twice the probable and 9 above 3.5 times (chance below .000001). Chance judged inadmissible in 4 of 6 series.
limits: Pre-modern statistics; no preregistration; sample size not stated in the text.
agent_relevance: The founding evidence was small and noisy, so identical elements is a prior, not a tested law.

source: Perkins & Salomon (1992) Transfer of learning, International Encyclopedia of Education (via secondary summary)
finding: Low-road transfer is automatic, triggered by surface similarity after varied practice. High-road transfer is deliberate abstraction, forward-reaching or backward-reaching. Hugging makes practice match the target. Bridging prompts for abstraction and connections.
numbers: No empirical numbers in the summary. The primary encyclopedia entry was not read.
limits: Wording of bridging is from secondary sources only.
agent_relevance: Hugging = store lessons in the same form as the target task. Bridging = an explicit step asking where else a lesson applies (SCHEMA O7).

source: Wikipedia: Transfer of learning
finding: Names the main frame: formal discipline (discredited), identical elements (1901), Guthrie's contiguity (expect little transfer, train under test conditions), near vs far, literal vs figural, low road vs high road, hugging and bridging.
numbers: The page reports no statistics.
limits: Encyclopedic; not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Vocabulary only. Useful for naming conditions in our class-to-class transfer test.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer: recap of the 1980 base rates
finding: With a hint to use a prior military story, about 75% solved the radiation problem; with no analogy under 10%. After memorising the story but with no hint, only about 30% solved it. So only a third or less of those able to apply the analogy noticed it.
numbers: Base rate about 10% (several replications). About 75% with hint, about 30% without. Noticing, not storage, was the bottleneck.
limits: These are the authors' recap of their 1980 work, not the 1980 tables (the 1980 PDF was blocked).
agent_relevance: A stored lesson that is correct but not retrieved is worth nothing. Retrieval cue design matters more than lesson quality.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Experiment 1, cord problem (pendulum solution)
finding: Same pattern in a second problem: a prior analogous story raised the pendulum solution to the two-cord problem.
numbers: N=69 high school students (grades 10-12): 25 analog-recall, 24 analog-summary, 20 control-summary. Before hint: analog groups 71% vs control 20%. Total after hint: 98% vs 30%. Recall vs summary did not differ (96 vs 100% total).
limits: Authors designed both story and problem; young sample.
agent_relevance: A hint to use the story took success to near ceiling. A cheap 'use the earlier example' prompt is a strong switch.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Experiment 2: adding an abstract principle
finding: Stating the abstract principle next to the story did not help. The principle alone also worked above base rate.
numbers: N=88 in 3 groups. Before hint: analog+principle 32% (N=31), analog only 29% (N=28), principle only 28% (N=29). Total: 80%, 79%, 66%. Not different (G2(2)=2.05, p=.36). All confidence limits excluded the 10% base rate.
limits: The principle was appended to the end of the story; subjects may have ignored it.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that adding a written rule to an example improves reuse. Test it; our lesson cards may gain nothing from an extra rule line.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Experiment 4: two analogs versus one
finding: Comparing two stories and writing how they are alike led to a schema and better transfer. Two analogs beat one analog plus an irrelevant control story.
numbers: N=98: two similar 28, two dissimilar 23, one analog plus control 47. Before hint: 39%, 52%, 21%. Total: 79%, 83%, 53%. Two-analog vs one: 45% vs 21% before hint (G2(1)=6.35, p<.01); 80% vs 53% total (G2(1)=8.36, p<.003).
limits: Gain relied on the written similarity description. Schema quality was scored by the authors.
agent_relevance: Supports storing lessons in pairs and forcing a compare step. Two cases plus a comparison beat one case.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) schema quality and transfer
finding: Quality of the induced schema was linked to transfer. Subjects who wrote a clear convergence schema from the two stories transferred more often.
numbers: Experiment 4: 45% of two-analog subjects solved before the hint vs 21% with one analog. The paper also tabulates schema levels in later experiments (exact cells not recorded here).
limits: Correlational within experiment: good schemas may reflect better solvers.
agent_relevance: Measure abstraction quality in code (does the lesson state a goal structure, not a story?) before relying on it for reuse.

source: Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: People retrieve old stories by surface similarity, but judge the best analogies by relational structure. Retrieval and soundness come apart.
numbers: Subjects read many stories; cue stories came about 2 weeks later in four match types: literal similarity (LS), surface similarity (SS), analogy (AN), first-order relations only (FOR). Retrievability order LS > SS > AN >= FOR. Soundness order AN > SS > surface only. Experiment 3: SS recalled 52%, object-attribute-only 17%, purely relational AN 7%.
quote: the failure was not of storage but of access
limits: Story materials in a laboratory memory task.
agent_relevance: Retrieval by surface embedding returns surface twins, not structural analogs. Index lessons by structure (goal, constraint, operator) as well.

source: Gentner et al. (1993) recognition control experiment
finding: Subjects stored relational structure, so the surface bias sits at retrieval, not encoding. In a choice task they picked the literal-similarity match 82% of the time (16.46 of 20).
numbers: Group 1 chose LS 82% (chi-square 61, df 12, p<.0001). Group 2, AN vs mere-appearance choice, was near chance: 55% picked the analogy.
limits: A choice task offers the analogical match as an option, so it is recognition, not retrieval.
agent_relevance: A two-stage design is supported: cheap wide recall first, then a structure-aware filter.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law MAC/FAC model, as reported in Gentner et al. (1993)
finding: MAC/FAC: stage one (MAC) is a cheap content-vector dot product over memory that keeps the best match and anything within 10% of it. Stage two (FAC) runs full structural alignment on the survivors.
numbers: Simulation memory held 36 stories (9 sets x 4 match types). With base stories as probes, MAC returned on average about 3.3 items and FAC accepted fewer. It reproduced the human order LS > SS > AN.
limits: Tiny simulated memory; story data, not real-world problems.
agent_relevance: A concrete retrieval design for the lesson library (feature-vector prefilter, then structural check), and a reason it still misses far analogs.

source: Singley & Anderson (1985) The transfer of text-editing skill
finding: Modern identical-elements test. Learning one line editor gave near total transfer to a second line editor, moderate transfer to a screen editor, and slight transfer from typing alone.
numbers: 24 computer-naive women, ages 18-30, from a secretarial school; about 500,000 keystrokes. Day-one savings on the second line editor: 150 s per edit (ED to EDT) vs 70 s (EDT to ED). Line editors to EMACS: about 35 s per edit saved, under half the line-editor-to-line-editor amount. Transfer subjects keyed at 1.1 s vs 2.3 s per keystroke on day one.
limits: Small cells (F tests on df 1,6). One skill domain. The authors note earlier editing work found analogies often misapplied.
agent_relevance: Transfer is large inside one family with shared operations and small across families. Do not expect cross-family reuse.

source: Singley & Anderson (1985; 1989 book) production-overlap model of transfer
finding: Formal identical elements: skill is a set of production rules; transfer is proportional to the shared rules, with a general and a specific component. Asymmetry follows because the smaller rule set is nearly a subset of the larger.
numbers: ED rules nearly a subset of EDT rules, so EDT-to-ED transfer exceeds ED-to-EDT. The specific component was 30% of the EMACS production set. Prior practice equivalent: about 2.0 days (EDT to ED) vs 1.8 days (ED to EDT).
limits: Two-component model fit to global measures, not keystrokes. Taatgen reports a model that fits amount of transfer better (secondary source).
agent_relevance: Predicts asymmetric transfer: a lesson from a harder class covers an easier class better than the reverse. Testable in class-to-class design.

source: Barnett & Ceci (2002) When and where do we apply what we learn? A taxonomy for far transfer
finding: A century of debate on far transfer has stalled because studies differ on many dimensions. They propose nine dimensions and argue that a single effect size for far transfer is misguided.
numbers: Psychological Bulletin 128(4), 612-637. Only the abstract was opened; no meta-numbers.
limits: Abstract only. The split into content dimensions and context dimensions is from background knowledge, not read here.
agent_relevance: Report each agent transfer test by dimension (domain, time gap, modality, framing), not as one near/far label.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training
finding: Three meta-analyses on children: far transfer effects shrink as control quality improves. Near transfer is robust.
numbers: Overall effects: chess 0.34 SD [0.24,0.44]; music 0.16 [0.09,0.22]; WM 0.12 [0.06,0.18]. Music far transfer: passive control 0.25 [0.17,0.34], k=64; active control 0.03 [-0.07,0.12], k=54. WM: passive 0.18, k=34; active 0.05 [-0.05,0.15], k=40. Chess active control 0.10 (one study). WM near transfer 0.46 passive, 0.44 active.
limits: Children and young adolescents; training programmes, not analogical problem solving. Critics say some music studies did not test real in-domain learning.
agent_relevance: Treat any apparent far-transfer gain of the agent as suspect until it beats an active control at equal tokens (SCHEMA G7).

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text analogy tasks, with human-like error patterns, except far story analogies.
numbers: Digit matrices, N=40 humans: GPT-3 above humans (OR=1.88, p=0.005). Letter strings N=57; verbal analogies N=57 (also Sternberg & Nigro N=20, Jones et al. N=241, SAT estimate). Story analogies N=54: humans beat GPT-3 (OR=0.37, p=0.0003); 15 of 54 humans chose the analogous story every trial. GPT-3 favoured the causal-relation story in the near condition (p=0.0039) but not the far one (p=0.065). GPT-4 preliminary: near-perfect near condition, better far.
quote: matching or even surpassing human capabilities in most settings
limits: Training-data overlap not excluded. Tests run inside one context window; no retrieval across episodes.
agent_relevance: Models find a given analog once it is in context. The open problem is getting the right analog into context.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) analogical problem solving section (radiation problem)
finding: Reproduced the Gick and Holyoak retrieval effect in GPT-3. With the general story plus the radiation problem it found the convergence solution. With two distractor stories added it did not, but did after a prompt to consider the earlier stories.
numbers: Qualitative case results (supplement S5.2-S5.5); no rate over many items.
limits: Single prompts, no counts. GPT-3 may know the radiation puzzle from training.
agent_relevance: Same bottleneck as humans: with distractors in context the model needs an explicit cue to look back. A bridging prompt is a lever.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Letter-string analogies in permuted or symbol alphabets: humans stay accurate, GPT models fall. On the original problems GPT was below humans, unlike in Webb et al.
numbers: 136 Prolific humans recruited. Overall accuracy: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773] (1,876 samples); GPT-3 0.488; GPT-3.5 0.350; GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Comprehension check: GPT-4 0.93-1.00 on successor/predecessor in altered alphabets.
limits: Letter-string domain only; zero-shot. Few-shot not tested. Humans scored higher than in Webb et al.
agent_relevance: Analogy skill seen on familiar surface forms is brittle under a surface change. Test lessons on re-skinned problems.

source: Hodel & West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Rebuttal in the style of a failed replication: GPT-3 does worse on simple variations of Webb et al.'s tasks, and human tests may not measure LLM ability.
numbers: On modified extend-sequence, successor/predecessor and fix-alphabet tasks GPT-3 fell well below the original level; only remove-redundant-letter and sort stayed in the original range. Comprehension checks: at least 30% of original level on all but one task.
limits: Variants designed by the authors; GPT-3 only. Training-data overlap is argued, not shown.
agent_relevance: A success on a published benchmark is not evidence of far transfer.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or reciting? Exploring the capabilities and limitations of language models through counterfactual tasks
finding: Across 11 task families (arithmetic, code, logic, spatial, chess, music, SET game), GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude and PaLM-2 fall on counterfactual variants of tasks they do well in default form.
numbers: 11 tasks. Example: base-9 vs base-10 addition; gaps sometimes near-perfect to near-zero for arithmetic. GPT-3.5 parseable programs fell from 99% default to 62%, 71% and 75% for flipped, 90-degree and 180-degree rotated settings. Models stayed above chance on counterfactuals, so some abstract ability exists.
limits: Prompted only; open models excluded. Default and counterfactual accuracy are correlated, a memorisation-like pattern.
agent_relevance: Skills learned in default form are narrow procedures. State the abstract rule and test lessons on counterfactual forms.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant examples and knowledge, then solves. It beats 0-shot CoT and often manual few-shot CoT on larger models.
limits: Gains are small on easy tasks (about 1-2 points on GSM8K for GPT-3.5). Weak models fail: davinci-001 retrieved 11% vs self-generated 9%.
agent_relevance: Self-generated analog examples are a cheap hugging step, but only for strong models.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) failure analysis of self-generated exemplars
finding: Manual analysis of 100 problems (50 solved, 50 failed) shows where analog use breaks.
numbers: Solved: 35/50 exemplars relevant and correct, 9/50 relevant but wrong, 6/50 irrelevant. Failed: 28/50 exemplars relevant and correct yet unsolved (12 generalization gap, 8 over-reliance on a specific exemplar, 8 other), 12/50 relevant but wrong, 10/50 irrelevant.
limits: Single analysis, GSM8K and MATH, GPT-3.5.
agent_relevance: Even good analogs fail in over half of failed cases. Check that the analog's structure fits the target before copying (G2, G3).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) scale effect and BIG-Bench
finding: The method needs scale. GSM8K self-generated exemplars: curie 2%, davinci-001 9%, davinci-002 48%, davinci-003 61%. Retrieved train-set exemplars: 3, 11, 47, 57%.
numbers: GPT-3.5 BIG-Bench, self-generated vs 0-shot CoT: word sorting 75.2 vs 67.6; logical deduction 41.6 vs 35.2; temporal sequences 57.6 vs 44.8 (3-shot CoT 58.0); colored objects 68.0 vs 61.6; formal fallacies 58.8 vs 55.6.
limits: Self-generation needs a model that has learned related problems; weak models make invalid exemplars.
agent_relevance: A library of earlier solved cases (retrieved) is safer than self-generation for weaker agents.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Language models, like humans, reason better when meaning supports the logical answer. Content leaks into abstract reasoning in both.
numbers: Three tasks: natural language inference, syllogism validity, Wason selection. Exact accuracies not extracted this session.
limits: Only abstract-level pattern recorded.
agent_relevance: A lesson is easier to reuse when its content looks like the target. Surface resemblance helps reuse and can also mislead (see Gentner).

source: Cross-source synthesis: three bottlenecks in transfer
finding: Noticing (retrieval by surface cue), mapping (aligning structure) and abstraction (inducing a schema) recur as failure points. Hints fix noticing; comparing two cases fixes abstraction; MAC/FAC separates the stages.
numbers: Gick and Holyoak: about 30% spontaneous vs 75% with hint; two-analog 80% vs 53%. Gentner: SS recalled 52% vs AN 7%.
limits: Synthesis of lab studies with stories; not LLM-tested in the same design.
agent_relevance: Design three separate agent steps (recall, map, abstract) and measure each.

source: Cross-source synthesis: LLM analogy results conflict
finding: Webb et al. (GPT-3 matches humans) conflicts with Lewis and Mitchell and Hodel and West (breaks under small changes) and Wu et al. (counterfactual gap). The difference is task familiarity.
numbers: Humans 0.753 vs GPT-4 0.452 on counterfactual letter strings; Webb et al. report GPT-3 above humans on original forms.
limits: Different task sets and human samples.
agent_relevance: Run transfer tests that change surface form while holding structure fixed. That is the near/far axis.

source: Cross-source synthesis: implications for O7 and lesson reuse
finding: Evidence supports: near transfer inside a task family is reliable; far transfer needs a prompt or compare step and is often absent; lesson cards should carry a structural key and a pair of examples.
numbers: Anchors: Singley and Anderson near total transfer between line editors, slight from typing; Gick and Holyoak 80% vs 53% for two analogs vs one; Sala and Gobet active-control far transfer about 0.03 to 0.05 SD.
limits: Our agent is not a human learner; these are design hypotheses to test.
agent_relevance: Test plan: lessons from class A on class B at equal tokens, with a bridging-prompt arm and a plain arm.
